text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

---Danish shipping and shipbuilding group J.Lauritzen's troubled Danyard shipping yard in northwest Denmark is having to arm itself with patience as the deal to sell half the yard to Malaysia's Penang Shipbuilding Construction (PSC) awaits the approval of the Malaysian authorities. The deadline for the sale is April 1 and the Malaysian authorities have still to okay the transferral of $100 million to the Danish group but PSC says there is no cause for alarm.
---Major growth in the Danish economy does not necessarily mean higher inflation or a lower current account surplus, leading bank Den Danske says in a new forecast.

---The prospect of Denmark not being able to participate in or shape a new joint European Union policy on asylum seekers and immigrants due to its 1993 Maastricht Treaty opt-out, is exercising Danish politicians' minds. Opposition Conservative leader Per Stig Moeller is calling for a national referendum on the issue either in the autumn or early 1998.

---When or if Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) goes on stream, countries like Denmark which do not participate will lose influence and find their scope for economic policy limited, former economic "wise man" Claus Vastrup says. Denmark opted out of EMU in its 1993 Maastricht Treaty referendum.
---Employees in telecommunications group Tele Danmark are now being offered retraining programmes. These could have prevented the need for mass redundancies recently announced by the firm.

---The left-wing in Danish politics is pressing the Social Democrat-led centre right coalition government to stick by Denmark's opt-outs on defence and monetary policy, legal and police cooperation and joint EU citizenship amid signs that the government might consider changing its stance after IGC is over and support joint cooperation on immigration, refugee and asylum policy with its EU partners.
